```{r}
#| label: knitr-opts
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(MultiStateTMLE)
```

As a running example, we ask how many deaths would be prevented by a drug that
makes an illness less likely.

# The Data

`illness_death` is a simulated trial with 200 patients who can fall ill and die,
and whose follow-up may be censored. The `illness` can happen at most once and
increases the hazard of death. Patients were randomised to `treatment` (`1`) or
placebo (`0`), and those with a higher baseline `biomarker` are more likely to
fall ill.

```{r}
#| label: data

head(illness_death)
```

Each row is one event, with the patient `id`, the `time` and type (`event`) of
the event, and the baseline covariates. Patient 3 died without falling ill and
has a single row, while patient 2 fell ill and then died and so has two:

```{r}
#| label: data-example

illness_death[illness_death$id %in% c(2, 3), ]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Simulated data"}
This is the format returned by `simevent::simulate_events()`, so data simulated
with [simevent](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/simevent) can be used directly.
`illness_death` was itself simulated with simevent, which means we can compare
the estimates with the true values later on.
:::

# Fitting the Hazards

We start by modelling the hazard of each event. `fit_initial()` takes one
formula per event, with the event on the left-hand side and the covariates on
the right. If another event appears as a covariate, it enters as the number of
such events so far. In `death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness`, the death
hazard therefore depends on whether the patient has fallen ill:

```{r}
#| label: fit-initial

models <- list(
  hazard_model(illness ~ biomarker + treatment, limit = 1),
  death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness,
  censoring ~ biomarker
)
fit <- fit_initial(illness_death, models = models, tau = 1)
fit
```

By default each hazard is a Cox model, so the death hazard is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
    \lambda_{\text{death}}(t) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\big(
     & \beta_1 \, \text{biomarker} + \beta_2 \, \text{treatment} \\
     & + \beta_3 \, \text{illness}(t) \big),
  \end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{illness}(t)$ is 1 after the patient has fallen ill and 0 before.
The argument `tau = 1` sets the time horizon, and all estimates below refer to
what has happened by time 1.

::: {.callout-note title="Hazard models"}
All events in the data need a model, including censoring. A plain formula is
shorthand for `hazard_model(formula)`. `hazard_model()` also has the arguments
`limit`, the maximum number of events per patient (one illness here), and
`at_risk`, a condition such as `~ illness == 0` specifying when patients are at
risk.
:::

# Halving the Illness Hazard

We first estimate the risk of death by time `tau` without any intervention. The
target is specified with `risk()`:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-observed

observed <- tmle_estimate(fit, risk(death))
observed
```

Now suppose the drug halves the illness hazard. `scale_intensity()` multiplies a
hazard by a factor $\alpha$, so the estimate below is the risk of death if the
illness hazard had been $\alpha \lambda_{\text{illness}}(t)$ with
$\alpha = 0.5$:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-halved

halved <- tmle_estimate(fit, risk(death), scale_intensity(illness = 0.5))
halved
```

Halving the illness hazard lowers the risk of death from
`{r} round(coef(observed), 3)` to `{r} round(coef(halved), 3)`. All other
hazards, including the death hazard after illness, are unchanged.

The estimate and confidence interval can be extracted with `coef()` and
`confint()`:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-ci

coef(halved)
confint(halved, level = 0.9)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Reading the output"}
The standard error is based on the efficient influence curve, so no bootstrap is
needed. The last line of the output is the estimate from the initial fit. TMLE
*targets* this estimate by updating the fitted hazards until the efficient
influence curve equation is solved. This removes the first-order bias of the
initial fit and gives valid confidence intervals, also when the hazards are
fitted with flexible models.

In this case no targeting steps were taken, because the Cox fits already solve
the equation within the stopping criterion $\text{se} / \log n$, and the final
estimate equals the initial one. This is common with 200 patients, where the
remaining bias is small compared with the standard error. With larger samples or
more flexible initial fits, one or more targeting steps are usually needed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Other interventions"}
A factor of `0` removes the illness entirely, and a factor above `1` makes it
more common. The factor can also be a formula in `time`, the baseline covariates
and the number of events so far. For example, the drug might only work early in
follow-up, or only in patients with `biomarker > 0`:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-time-varying

coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  scale_intensity(illness = ~ ifelse(time < 0.5, 0.5, 1))
))
coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  scale_intensity(illness = ~ ifelse(biomarker > 0, 0.5, 1))
))
```

Several hazards can be scaled at once, e.g.
`scale_intensity(illness = 0.5, death = 0.8)`.
:::

# From Hazards to Risks

A halved hazard is not easy to interpret, since it does not directly say how
many fewer patients fall ill. `intervention_curve()` estimates, for a grid of
factors $\alpha$, both the risk of illness (the *exposure*) and the risk of
death:

```{r}
#| label: intervention-curve

curve <- intervention_curve(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  exposure = risk(illness),
  alpha = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)
)
curve
```

Plotting the risk of death against the risk of illness shows how the two are
related:

```{r}
#| label: intervention-plot
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Estimated risk of death plotted against the estimated risk of illness
#|   across interventions on the illness hazard, with 95% confidence intervals.
#|   The risk of death increases with the risk of illness.

ce <- curve$estimate

plot(
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$estimate,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  las = 1,
  bty = "l",
  ylim = range(ce$lower, ce$upper),
  xlab = "Risk of illness by time 1",
  ylab = "Risk of death by time 1"
)
arrows(
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$lower,
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$upper,
  angle = 90,
  code = 3,
  length = 0.04
)
```

Removing the illness entirely (the leftmost point) lowers the risk of death by
about `{r} round(100 * (coef(observed) - ce$estimate[1]))` percentage points.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Checking against the truth"}
Since `illness_death` was simulated from the model below, simevent can compute
the true risks under each intervention. We simulate a large number of patients
without censoring, with the illness hazard scaled through `intervene`:

```{r}
#| label: truth
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("simevent", quietly = TRUE)

library(simevent)

true_model <- sim_model(
  biomarker = sim_covariate(function(N) rnorm(N)),
  treatment = sim_covariate(function(N) rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)),
  illness = sim_process("transient", limit = 1, eta = 0.7, nu = 1),
  death = sim_process("terminal", eta = 0.3, nu = 1),
  censoring = sim_process("censoring", eta = 0.1, nu = 1),
  effects = list(
    sim_effect(illness ~ biomarker + treatment, coef = c(0.5, -1)),
    sim_effect(death ~ illness + treatment, coef = c(1.2, -0.3))
  )
)

true_risks <- function(intervene) {
  sim <- simulate_events(
    true_model,
    n = 1e5,
    cens = 0,
    intervene = intervene,
    seed = 1
  )
  risks <- event_risk(sim, true_model, c("illness", "death"), tau = 1)
  setNames(risks$risk, risks$process)
}

check <- ce[, c("alpha", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
check$truth <- sapply(
  check$alpha,
  function(alpha) true_risks(list(illness = alpha))["death"]
)
check
```

All intervals cover the true values, and the estimates are close to the true
curve, including when the illness is removed.
:::

# Calibrating the Drug

The question is often phrased in terms of risks rather than hazards, for example
what would happen if the drug prevented 20% of illnesses. `calibrate()` finds
the factor $\alpha$ at which the risk of illness reaches a given value and
estimates the risk of death under that intervention:

```{r}
#| label: calibrate

calibrated <- tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
)
calibrated
```

The first table shows the calibrated $\alpha$ and the resulting risk of illness
$\theta$, which is 80% of the observed
`{r} round(ce$exposure_estimate[ce$alpha == 1], 3)`. The second table shows the
risk of death under this intervention.

::: {.callout-note title="Calibration rules"}
There are three ways to specify the target risk of illness:

- `level(theta)`: the risk equals `theta`.
- `absolute_change(delta)`: the observed risk plus `delta`.
- `relative_change(rho)`: the observed risk times `rho`.

Since $\alpha$ is estimated, the standard error `se` takes its uncertainty into
account, while `se_crude` treats $\alpha$ as known.
:::

`years_lost()` can be used in place of `risk()` to estimate the expected years
of life lost before `tau`:

```{r}
#| label: calibrate-years-lost

coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  years_lost(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
))
```

# Explaining a Treatment Effect

Up to now, `treatment` has only entered as a covariate. Suppose we instead want
to estimate its effect on death, and how much of that effect is due to treated
patients falling ill less often. The calibrated intervention from the previous
section can be used for this. Treated patients are given the risk of illness
they would have had on placebo, and the total effect is split into two
contrasts:

- the *mediated* effect, comparing treatment with the calibrated intervention,
  which is the part of the effect that goes through the illness, and
- the *calibrated* effect, comparing the calibrated intervention with placebo,
  which is the remaining part.

To estimate under everyone treated or everyone on placebo, `fit_initial()` also
needs a model for how treatment was assigned, given in `treatment_model`:

```{r}
#| label: trial-fit

trial_fit <- fit_initial(
  illness_death,
  models = models,
  tau = 1,
  treatment_model = treatment ~ biomarker
)
```

The argument `a` sets the treatment for everyone, and `reference_a = 0`
calibrates the risk of illness to its value under placebo:

```{r}
#| label: trial-arms

treated <- tmle_estimate(trial_fit, risk(death), a = 1)
placebo <- tmle_estimate(trial_fit, risk(death), a = 0)
treated_calibrated <- tmle_estimate(
  trial_fit,
  risk(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(1), reference_a = 0),
  a = 1
)
treated_calibrated
```

Giving treated patients the risk of illness they would have had on placebo
requires multiplying their illness hazard by about
`{r} round(treated_calibrated$calibration$estimate[1], 1)`. The three fits are
combined with `calibrated_contrasts()`:

```{r}
#| label: trial-contrasts

contrasts <- calibrated_contrasts(treated, placebo, treated_calibrated)
contrasts
```

Treatment lowers the risk of death by
`{r} round(-100 * contrasts$estimate$estimate[1])` percentage points, and
`{r} round(-100 * contrasts$estimate$estimate[2])` of these are mediated through
the illness.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Checking against the truth"}
Using `true_model` from earlier, simevent can also give the true contrasts. Each
arm is simulated without censoring, and for the calibrated arm we search for the
factor on the illness hazard that gives the same risk of illness as on placebo:

```{r}
#| label: trial-truth
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("simevent", quietly = TRUE)

placebo_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 0))
treatment_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1))
true_alpha <- uniroot(
  function(alpha) {
    calibrated <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1, illness = alpha))
    calibrated["illness"] - placebo_risks["illness"]
  },
  interval = c(1, 5),
  tol = 0.01
)$root
calibrated_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1, illness = true_alpha))

check <- contrasts$estimate[, c("contrast", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
check$truth <- c(
  treatment_risks["death"] - placebo_risks["death"],
  treatment_risks["death"] - calibrated_risks["death"],
  calibrated_risks["death"] - placebo_risks["death"]
)
check
```

All intervals cover the true values. The contrasts are estimated less precisely
than the risks, since each one compares two arms of about 100 patients.
:::

# Next Steps

- `risk()` and `years_lost()` can take several events, as in
  `risk(death, illness)`, and can be restricted to events occurring in certain
  states, as in `risk(death, when = ~ illness == 0)`. For recurrent events they
  give the expected number of events, or the risk of a first event with
  `only_first = TRUE`. See `?"target-parameters"`.
- For simulating event history data and computing true values under
  interventions, see [simevent](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/simevent).
